intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene on chromosome 19.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a novel homozygous variant in CCDC9 (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C>T, NM_015603.3, NP_056418.1: p. Ser109Leu) in a patient from a consanguineous family.
checks.explanation: Abstract reports a homozygous CCDC9 variant in severe asthenozoospermia but calls CCDC9 only a candidate gene that 'may be' pathogenic; the name SPGF104 is not used.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 gene is located on chromosome 19.
checks.explanation: NC_000019.9 is the chromosome 19 reference sequence; the chromosomal location is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility marked by severe asthenozoospermia, in which fewer than 1% of spermatozoa in the ejaculated semen are motile (Sha et al., 2019). Sperm from an affected man also had severely damaged morphology and ultrastructure (Sha et al., 2019).

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility characterized by severe asthenozoospermia.
checks.evidence_quote: Therefore, CCDC9 may be a novel pathogenic gene associated with severe asthenozoospermia.
checks.explanation: Severe asthenozoospermia and male reproductive health are described, but the SPGF104 designation does not appear in the abstract.

checks.claim: In SPGF104, fewer than 1% of spermatozoa in the ejaculated semen are motile.
checks.evidence_quote: Owing to less than 1% of motile spermatozoa in the ejaculated semen, severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat to the male reproductive health.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives this as the definition of severe asthenozoospermia in general.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) recruited 7 large families from rural Pakistan with clinically diagnosed male infertility, 5 of them with a history of consanguinity. One of these families carried biallelic variants in CCDC9.

checks.claim: Five of the 7 Pakistani male infertility families recruited by Khan et al. (2025) had a history of consanguinity.
checks.evidence_quote: We recruited seven large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, including five with a history of consanguinity.

checks.claim: One of the 7 Pakistani male infertility families studied by Khan et al. (2025) carried biallelic variants in CCDC9.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified plausible genetic causes in five of the seven families, including a homozygous 10 kb deletion of exon 2 in a well-established male infertility gene (M1AP), and biallelic missense substitutions (SPAG6, CCDC9, TUBA3C)
checks.explanation: Five genes are listed for five families, so one family carries the biallelic CCDC9 variants.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SPGF104 is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Sha et al. (2019) found a homozygous CCDC9 mutation in an affected man from a consanguineous family, and Khan et al. (2025) found biallelic CCDC9 variants in a Pakistani family with male infertility.

checks.explanation: A homozygous variant in a consanguineous family fits recessive inheritance, but the abstract does not state the inheritance pattern.

paragraphs.text: In a man from a consanguineous family who had severe asthenozoospermia, Sha et al. (2019) identified a homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene (g.47763960C-T, NC_000019.9) that caused a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution. In silico analysis predicted that the variant was highly pathogenic. CCDC9 protein levels were significantly reduced in the patient's spermatozoa.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 g.47763960C-T (NC_000019.9) mutation causes a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was highly pathogenic and was predicted to be a candidate gene for asthenozoospermia through in silico analysis.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) performed whole-genome sequencing on 26 individuals (3 to 5 per family) from 7 large Pakistani families with male infertility. In 1 family they identified biallelic missense substitutions in the CCDC9 gene. The abstract does not give the specific variants.

paragraphs.text: In a man from a consanguineous family who had severe asthenozoospermia (SPGF104), Sha et al. (2019) identified a homozygous C-to-T change in the CCDC9 gene (g.47763960C-T, NC_000019.9), resulting in a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution. In silico analysis predicted that the variant was highly pathogenic. CCDC9 protein levels were significantly reduced in the patient's spermatozoa, and the sperm had severely damaged morphology and ultrastructure.
